name: Badimaya
confidence_why: 2 independent first-hand sources agree (1 agree, 0 refine), none contradicts
catalog_quote: Primary stress is initial, as in: /wanara/ long, thin /windyindyi/ grasshopper. In words of four or five syllables, a weaker secondary stress occurs on the third syllable from the front: /ngan.ganguwa/ to choke on something /wanaldyilinga/ scorpion. This suggests an alternating stress pattern ... Unfortunately, no words of more than five syllables, necessary to test this hypothesis, are extant.

new_statements.quote: Word stress is usually on the first syllable, so it is the first part of the word that sounds the loudest. For example, in the English word 'radio', stress occurs on the first part of the word 'radio', in 'retire' stress occurs in the second part of the word.
new_statements.citation: Thieberger, Nicholas (1996). Handbook of Western Australian Aboriginal Languages South of the Kimberley Region. Pacific Linguistics, Australian National University.
new_statements.locator: Chapter 1 Introduction, section 1.5 'Spelling of the language names' (pronunciation guide), printed p. 6 (PDF page 14). The Badimaya entry itself is section 4.3.2, printed pp. 76-77 (PDF pages 84-85).
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (416 pp., text layer). extracted text of PDF page 14 = printed p. 6 gives exactly: 'Word stress is usually on the first syllable, so it is the first part of the word that sounds the loudest. For example, in the English word 'radio', stress occurs on the first part of the word 'radio', in 'retire' stress occurs in the second part of the word.' (only difference: a stray scanned space before the comma after the second 'radio'). Locator refinement: the sentence sits in subsection 1.5.1 'Pronunciation guide' (heading on printed p. 5, PDF page 13), inside section 1.5 'Spelling of the language names'; the reader's locator names 1.5 with '(pronunciation guide)' in parentheses, which is close…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's initial primary stress (StressTyp2 stress placement coded per word length as 10 100 1010 (1 = a stressed syllable)), but it is a region-wide generalization from the introduction, not a statement about Badimaya, and it says nothing about the alternating secondary stresses the catalog records. Weak corroboration only; the real primary source for Badimaya stress is Dunn 1982/1988, which this handbook cites but is not among the listed open works.
new_statements.rule_in_words: A blanket statement in the handbook's pronunciation guide covering Western Australian Aboriginal languages generally: primary word stress is usually on the first syllable. The Badimaya entry (4.3.2, pp. 76-77) has no phonology or stress information at all; it lists names, classification (O'Grady, Voegelin & Voegelin 1966: Kardu), speaker numbers, and materials, and points to Dunn (1982 MA thesis; 1988, Pacific Linguistics A-71, pp. 19-149) as the only grammar.
new_statements.exceptions: Only the hedge 'usually'; no language-specific exceptions given.
new_statements.identity_note: The handbook entry is for Badimaya as a whole (names Badi-maia, Badimaia, Badimara, Barimaia, Bidungu, Patimara, Patimay, Wallawe, Wardal, Yamadgee, Yamaji; 'Dialects of the language: No information'). The opened copy is the 1993 Pacific Linguistics C-124 print edition, of which the 1996 coombs.anu.edu.au web version listed by Glottolog was a revision; the web version is offline (404) and its Internet Archive copy could not be reached by automated download.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: The classification (fixed-strict, initial primary, secondary on σ3 in 4-5σ words, no final stress; withdrawn as a Maranungku attestation) matches Dunn 1988:34 exactly, and the quotation is verbatim at the stated page in the open-access PDF we hold. Dunn 1988 is the sole grammar of Badimaya and the root of every database entry; no later phonological or instrumental work exists (checked Glottolog list, Bednall's publication list, CDU repository, general web search). The only housekeeping point: the record's formal 'quote'/'cite'/'loc'/'grade' fields are blank while the evidence sits in 'the domain quotation'/'the domain locator' — promote Dunn 1988:34 §2.3 into the cite/quote fields and assign a grade.
